# I Built an AI That Writes Full Documentation for Any GitHub Repository — and It Costs Me $0.50 per 100 Repos

**TL;DR:** Paste a GitHub repo URL → get a complete, professional README + developer documentation (architecture, features, API overview, FAQ, best practices) as Markdown and PDF in under 60 seconds — generated by an LLM that actually reads your code, not just the README. Open-source, runs locally, costs pennies.

## The Problem

Every developer knows the pain: you clone a repo, and the README is either missing, three years old, or says "WIP, docs coming soon." Even with good docs, you still have to read thousands of lines of code to understand the architecture, the entry points, the configuration, the dependencies, and how the modules actually fit together.

Writing good documentation is boring, slow, and nobody wants to do it — especially for side projects. So I built a tool that does it automatically.

## What It Does

**Input:** A public GitHub repository URL.

**Output, in ~1 minute:**
- A clean, professional README
- Full developer documentation with:
  - Project overview and purpose
  - Features (inferred from actual code)
  - Architecture overview + patterns
  - Folder structure tree
  - Installation & quick-start commands (auto-detects npm/pip/poetry/go/cargo)
  - Configuration file explanations
  - Full dependency list
  - "How it works" narrative grounded in real source files
  - Key modules with paths and roles
  - API overview when detected
  - Best practices + future improvements
  - FAQ

All exported as both **Markdown** and a **styled PDF**.

## How It Works — The Pipeline

The app is a Flask web app orchestrating an agent pipeline built on LangGraph:

```
GitHub URL → Validate → Clone (GitPython) → Parse → LLM Analysis → Documentation Generator → LLM Review → Markdown → PDF
```

**1. Fetch & Parse (deterministic, no AI)**
- Fetches repo metadata via the GitHub REST API
- Clones the repo
- Parses README, config files, dependencies, entry points
- Ignores node_modules, dist, build artifacts, binary files

**2. AI Analysis (the interesting part)**
This is where most "AI docs" tools cheat — they just feed the README to an LLM and hope. This one sends the LLM:
- The README
- A compact file inventory (path, language, size)
- **Source excerpts of the most relevant files** (entry points, services, models, agents — filtered to skip tests, lockfiles, docs, generated code)

The LLM (DeepSeek) returns structured JSON: description, architecture, key modules, features, how-it-works, configuration, API overview, FAQ. Parsed dependencies and entry points are then merged back in authoritatively so the LLM can't drop or hallucinate them.

**3. Documentation Generation**
A template renders the structured knowledge into a full, consistent Markdown document with a professional folder-structure tree.

**4. LLM Review Pass**
A second LLM call proofreads the document — fixes grammar, normalizes formatting, keeps the section structure. It's optional and gracefully skipped if the doc exceeds the token budget.

**5. Export**
Markdown + styled PDF (via WeasyPrint).

## The "Free Tier" War Story

The first version used **Groq's free tier** (8k TPM). A real-world repo with 420 files instantly blew the token budget — every request returned HTTP 413 "Request too large" and the pipeline silently fell back to deterministic template docs (fake AI output!). The fix:

- **Token-budgeted prompt building** — tiered content limits: the prompt renders at full size first, then progressively trims source excerpts, file inventory, and README until it fits under the limit. Verified: a 420-file repo now produces a ~6.6k-token prompt instead of ~9.3k.
- **DeepSeek as the provider** — OpenAI-compatible, 64k context, generous rate limits. $5 of credits ≈ 15-18 million input tokens ≈ documentation for ~100+ repos. Effectively free.
- **Deterministic fallback everywhere** — if the LLM fails, the pipeline produces accurate-but-generic docs from parsing alone instead of crashing. No dead ends.

Lesson: **always size your prompts for the cheapest tier, and always have a fallback that isn't the LLM.**

## Why "LLM reads source excerpts" matters

Anecdotally, the quality difference is night and day:
- Without excerpts: "This is a Python application with a Flask structure." (useless)
- With excerpts: "The application initializes in `app.py`, routes requests through `services/llm_service.py`, orchestrates agents in `agents/graph.py` via LangGraph, and persists output through `services/pdf_service.py`. Dependencies are declared in requirements.txt." (actually useful)

## Stack

- **Backend:** Python 3.12, Flask, LangGraph, GitPython, PyGithub
- **LLM:** DeepSeek (any OpenAI-compatible provider works — Groq, OpenAI, etc.)
- **Parsing:** Custom repository parser (language, deps, entry points, config)
- **Export:** Python-Markdown + WeasyPrint PDF
- **UI:** Tailwind dashboard, no build step
- **Deploy:** Dockerfile + Render config included

## Run It Yourself

```bash
git clone <this repo>
cd github-doc-ai
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env   # add DEEPSEEK_API_KEY (or any OpenAI-compatible key)
python app.py          # open http://localhost:5000
```

Paste any public GitHub repo URL and hit Analyze.

## Use Cases

- **Oss maintainers:** instantly generate/refresh README + docs for your projects
- **Teams onboarding:** point new hires at generated docs instead of "go read the code"
- **Hackathon/jam submissions:** get decent documentation without spending the last hour writing it
- **Learning:** understand any unfamiliar repo's architecture in one page
- **Blog content:** it's the first module of a larger content platform — the same knowledge object can feed blog posts, LinkedIn posts, X threads, tutorials, and presentations
